SA06:C.4r: C.4r (Proved: a single integral numerical surface class detects the remaining cases).. Let $A$ be an abelian variety of dimension $g\in\{2,3\}$ over an algebraically closed field $k$ of arbitrary characteristic. Put $X=A\times\widehat A$, write $P=c_1(\mathcal P_A)$, and set \[ N^r(X)=\mathrm{CH}^r(X)/{\equiv_{\mathrm{num}}}, \qquad r=2g-2, \] with integral coefficients. We regard this torsion-free group as a subgroup of $N^r(X)_{\mathbb Q}$. The following are equivalent: \begin{enumerate} \item $A$ is an actual direct summand of a product of Jacobians; \item the rational numerical class \[ \gamma_A=\frac{P^{2g-2}}{(2g-2)!} \in N^{2g-2}(X)_{\mathbb Q} \] belongs to the integral numerical lattice $N^{2g-2}(X)$. \end{enumerate} Thus we require an integral dimension-two cycle numerically equivalent to $P^2/2$ for a surface, or to $P^4/24$ for a threefold. Over $\mathbb C$ the same conditions are also equivalent to integral algebraicity of the corresponding integral Hodge class.

SA06:C.4ab: C.4ab (Proved: a partial Fourier test for the surface case).. \emph{Status: proved criterion and method exclusion. This is an equivalent formulation of the residual splitting problem, not a solution of that problem or a claim of priority.} Let $A$ be a complex abelian surface with a primitive polarization $\ell=c_1(L)$ of type $(1,2)$, and assume \[ \operatorname{NS}(A)=\mathbb Z\ell,\qquad \operatorname{End}_{\mathrm{HS}}H^1(A,\mathbb Q)=\mathbb Q, \qquad \operatorname{End}_{\mathrm{HS}}T(A)_{\mathbb Q}=\mathbb Q, \] Here we put $T(A)_{\mathbb Q}=\ell^\perp\subset H^2(A,\mathbb Q)$. The last condition is an explicit assumption. We do not infer it from a claim about a special surface. These hypotheses include the Mumford--Tate general case, in the sense of \citet[p.~2473]{cyVoisin2024}. Both relevant symplectic representations are absolutely irreducible: the standard one and the primitive part of its second exterior power. Put \[ X=A\times\widehat A,\qquad P=c_1(\mathcal P_A),\qquad \ell_1=\operatorname{pr}_A^*\ell, \quad \ell_2=\operatorname{pr}_{\widehat A}^*\widehat\ell, \] where the primitive dual polarization satisfies $\lambda_{\widehat\ell}\lambda_\ell=[2]_A$. For an integral cycle $Z\in\mathrm{CH}^2(A\times A)$, we use the convention \[ Z^*\alpha=(p_1)_*\bigl([Z]\smile p_2^*\alpha\bigr). \] There are integers $t,s,n$ such that $Z^*$ acts by $t$ on $H^1(A,\mathbb Q)$, by $s$ on $T(A)_{\mathbb Q}$, and by $n$ on $\mathbb Q\ell$. The following conditions are equivalent: \begin{enumerate} \item $A$ is an actual direct summand of a product of Jacobians; \item some integral $Z\in\mathrm{CH}^2(A\times A)$ has $t-s$ odd. \end{enumerate} More precisely, for every such $Z$ we construct an integral curve cycle on $X$ whose mixed Matsusaka endomorphism is \[ m_Z\operatorname{id}_A, \qquad m_Z=3(t^2-s)-\frac{n-s}{2}, \qquad m_Z\equiv t-s\pmod2. \tag{PF.1} \] The integer $m_Z$ is an actual integral coefficient, not the coefficient of a rationally divided Chern character. \emph{Step 1: the integral gluing condition.} The action of an integral correspondence preserves integral cohomology. The Hodge-endomorphism assumptions therefore make $t,s,n$ integers: each scalar preserves a nonzero free lattice, and $\ell$ is primitive. There are no rational Hodge homomorphisms between $T(A)_{\mathbb Q}$ and $\mathbb Q\ell$. Indeed a map in one direction would give a rational Hodge class in $T(A)$, and duality gives the same conclusion in the other direction. The lattice $H^2(A,\mathbb Z)$ is unimodular, and $\ell^2=4$. Choose $w$ in this lattice with $(w,\ell)=1$. The decomposition of $Z^*$ into its two rational eigenspaces gives \[ Z^*w-sw=\frac{n-s}{4}\ell. \] The left side is integral, and $\ell$ is primitive. Consequently \[ n-s\in4\mathbb Z. \tag{PF.2} \] Write $\Delta_{22}$ for the $(2,2)$ component of the diagonal. The same component of $[Z]$ is \[ s\Delta_{22}+\frac{n-s}{4}\ell\boxtimes\ell. \tag{PF.3} \] Its $(1,3)$ component is $t\Delta_{13}$. \emph{Step 2: an integral Fourier construction.} Write $Z=\sum_i m_iZ_i$ and choose resolutions $f_i:\widetilde Z_i\to Z_i\hookrightarrow A\times A$. The integral class \[ K_Z=\sum_i m_i(f_i)_*[\mathcal O_{\widetilde Z_i}] \in K_0(A\times A) \] has $\operatorname{ch}_0(K_Z)=\operatorname{ch}_1(K_Z)=0$ and $\operatorname{ch}_2(K_Z)=[Z]$. Indeed, such a projector has $t=1,s=0$, so the forward construction applies. Conversely the normalized divisor $D_i$ above has only the component $H^1(A)\otimes H^1(C_i)$. SA06:C.4r: C.4r (Proved: a single integral numerical surface class detects the remaining cases).. Let $A$ be an abelian variety of dimension $g\in\{2,3\}$ over an algebraically closed field $k$ of arbitrary characteristic. Put $X=A\times\widehat A$, write $P=c_1(\mathcal P_A)$, and set \[ N^r(X)=\mathrm{CH}^r(X)/{\equiv_{\mathrm{num}}}, \qquad r=2g-2, \] with integral coefficients. We regard this torsion-free group as a subgroup of $N^r(X)_{\mathbb Q}$. The following are equivalent: \begin{enumerate} \item $A$ is an actual direct summand of a product of Jacobians; \item the rational numerical class \[ \gamma_A=\frac{P^{2g-2}}{(2g-2)!} \in N^{2g-2}(X)_{\mathbb Q} \] belongs to the integral numerical lattice $N^{2g-2}(X)$. \end{enumerate} Thus we require an integral dimension-two cycle numerically equivalent to $P^2/2$ for a surface, or to $P^4/24$ for a threefold. Over $\mathbb C$ the same conditions are also equivalent to integral algebraicity of the corresponding integral Hodge class.

SA06:C.4u: C.4u (Proved: all supersingular threefolds in characteristic at least five).. Every supersingular abelian threefold over an algebraically closed field of characteristic \(p\ge5\) is an actual direct summand of a product of Jacobians. In characteristics two and three we obtain, respectively, \[ s_J(A)\mid2\quad(p=2),\qquad s_J(A)\mid3\quad(p=3); \] these two divisibilities do not by themselves prove a retraction. More generally, for a supersingular abelian variety \(A\) of dimension \(g\ge1\), \begin{equation} s_J(A)\mid p^{\,v_p((2g-1)!)}. \end{equation} In particular every such \(A\) is a direct summand if \(p>2g-1\).

SA06:C.4y: C.4y (Proved): a parity obstruction for semihomogeneous Chern constructions.. Let $A/\mathbb C$ be an abelian surface with $\operatorname{End}(A)=\mathbb Z$ and a primitive polarization $L$ of type $(1,2)$. Let $R_{\rm sh}$ be the integral graded subring of numerical cycle classes on $X$ generated by the Chern classes of all semihomogeneous vector bundles on $X$. Then \[ P^2/2\notin R_{\rm sh}^{2}. \] Moreover, the mixed Matsusaka coefficient of every class in $R_{\rm sh}^{3}$ is even. Here we normalize the mixed coefficient to take the value $1$ on $P^3/6$; an overall change of Poincar\'e sign does not change the parity assertion. These statements rule out this construction of the missing class in C.4r. They assert nothing about arbitrary algebraic cycles or arbitrary vector bundles on $X$.

The tangent bundle of an abelian variety is trivial, so the cohomological transform is \[ \mathcal F_x(u)=(q_{a,y})_* \bigl(p_{a,x}^*u\,e^{P_{x,y}}\bigr). \] We fix the usual normalized Poincar\'e sign, for which \[ \mathcal F_x(\Delta_{13})=P,\qquad \mathcal F_x(\Delta_{22})=P^2/2,\qquad \mathcal F_x(\ell_x)=-\widehat\ell_y. \tag{PF.5} \] These identities can also be checked directly in the exterior algebra on $H^1(A_a)\oplus H^1(A_x)\oplus H^1(\widehat A_y)$. For an integral basis, write \[ \ell_a=a_0a_1+2a_2a_3,\qquad \widehat\ell_y=2y_0y_1+y_2y_3,\qquad P_{a,y}=\sum_{j=0}^3a_jy_j. \] Multiplying $\prod_{j=0}^3(x_j-a_j)$ by $\exp(\sum_jx_jy_j)$ and integrating the four $x_j$ gives $\exp(P_{a,y})$, including every sign in (PF.5). The Fourier transform takes bidegree $(a,b)$ to $(a,4-b)$. Since $K_Z$ has no Chern-character components of degrees zero or one, this gives \[ c_1(E_Z)=a\ell_1+tP\quad (a\in\mathbb Z). \] In particular there is no $\ell_2$ term: it could only come from the vanished $(0,2)$ component of $\operatorname{ch}_1(K_Z)$. The $(2,2)$ component of $\operatorname{ch}_2(E_Z)$ is, by (PF.3)--(PF.5), \[ s\frac{P^2}{2}-\frac{n-s}{4}\ell_1\ell_2. \] Therefore the $(2,2)$ component of $c_2(E_Z)$ is \[ \frac{t^2-s}{2}P^2+\frac{n-s}{4}\ell_1\ell_2. \tag{PF.6} \] All the omitted components have different bidegrees; after intersection with $P$, they cannot contribute to $H^3(A)\otimes H^3(\widehat A)$, which is the component controlling the mixed endomorphism. \emph{Step 3: the mixed integer.} In the same exterior basis we have \[ P^3=-3\ell_1\ell_2P. \tag{PF.7} \] The integral cohomology class $P^3/6$ has mixed Matsusaka endomorphism $\operatorname{id}_A$. This is the unimodular Poincar\'e normalization already used in C.4i and C.4r; it does not assert that $P^3/6$ is an integral Chow class. For the actual integral curve \[ z_Z=c_2(E_Z)\cdot P \in\mathrm{CH}^3(X), \] (PF.6)--(PF.7) give (PF.1). By (PF.2), its second summand is even, while $t^2\equiv t\pmod2$. Each normalized curve component of $z_Z$ supplies a factorization of its mixed endomorphism through its Jacobian. Thus $m_Z\in I_J(A)$. If $t-s$ is odd, $m_Z$ is odd. C.4n gives $2\in I_J(A)$, and B\'ezout gives $1\in I_J(A)$, proving (1). \emph{Step 4: the converse is integral.} Suppose that there are curves $C_i$ and homomorphisms \[ u_i:A\to J(C_i),\qquad v_i:J(C_i)\to A, \qquad \sum_i v_i u_i=\operatorname{id}_A. \] Choose a point on each curve and the corresponding Abel map $a_i:C_i\to J(C_i)$. Pull the normalized Poincar\'e line bundle on $J(C_i)\times C_i$ back by $u_i\times\operatorname{id}_{C_i}$; let its integral divisor class be $D_i\in\mathrm{CH}^1(A\times C_i)$. Set \[ Z=\sum_i (\operatorname{id}_A\times(v_i a_i))_*D_i \in\mathrm{CH}^2(A\times A). \] The action on $H^1$ is $\sum_i u_i^*v_i^*=(\sum_i v_i u_i)^*=\operatorname{id}$. The action on $T(A)$ factors through $H^2(C_i,\mathbb Q)$, a Tate Hodge structure, and is zero. Hence $t=1,s=0$. No division, isogeny inverse, or saturation of a cycle group enters this construction. This proves the equivalence. In this precise surface scope the conditions are also equivalent to integral algebraicity of the first K\"unneth projector $\delta_1$, namely ``splitness'' in \citet[Definition 1.9, p.~2473]{cyVoisin2024}. Indeed, such a projector has $t=1,s=0$, so the forward construction applies. Conversely the normalized divisor $D_i$ above has only the component $H^1(A)\otimes H^1(C_i)$. Its pushforward therefore has only component $(1,3)$, and the sum acts as the identity on $H^1$. Thus its cohomology class is exactly $\delta_1$. We assert this equivalence only under the stated surface hypotheses, not for abelian varieties of arbitrary dimension. \emph{Step 5: the known residual fibre-product surface fails this test.} Suppose $\pi:S\to A$ is a composition of blowups and $\gamma:S\to Y$ is a generically finite morphism to a smooth projective surface whose $H^1$ is zero and whose $H^2$ is generated by divisor classes. Assume that $\gamma$ is finite and generically separable. The cycle of its fibre product is \[ [S\times_Y S]=[\Delta_S]+[W], \] where $W$ is the residual correspondence, with its natural cycle multiplicities. Its action is $\gamma^*\gamma_*-\operatorname{id}$. The first term is zero on $H^1(S)$ and on $T(S)$. Pushing $W$ to $A\times A$ therefore gives $t=s=-1$, so the mixed integer of its partial Fourier construction is even. The same conclusion holds for integral sums of these correspondences, multiplication graphs, and exterior products of divisors: the parity $t-s$ is additive and vanishes on each. This applies directly to the Galois-closure surface of \citet[Proposition 4.5 and \S5, (5.1), author pp.~16--18] {frC4BastianelliPirolaStoppino2010}: their resolved abelian surface maps finitely with degree three to the rational ruled surface $\mathbb F_3$, and their surface is the residual fibre product. Its full-span Albanese property alone would not justify this Fourier exclusion; the residual-correspondence calculation does. We make no assertion here about every codimension-two cycle on $A\times A$ or every Fourier transform of an arbitrary sheaf. \emph{Exact verification and remaining issue.} We retain the rational exterior-algebra program \begin{center} \texttt{check\_partial\_fourier\_parity.py}. \end{center} It checks (PF.5), (PF.7), the full diagonal Fourier identity, 4,913 integral parity cases, and 41 multiplication graphs using rational exterior algebra. Its saved output records the actual runtime. The proof of the universal identities is the exterior calculation and the displayed formulas; finite testing is only a check of their signs and implementation. The remaining mathematical issue is the existence of an integral algebraic correspondence with $t-s$ odd. Since the converse above shows this issue is equivalent to the original splitting assertion, the criterion is recorded as a reformulation and a concrete method exclusion, not as movement of the unresolved main gate. For comparison, the new \emph{\'etale} integral projectors of \citet[Theorem 1.7, Corollary 1.8, and \S B.6]{cyKahnDivided2026PF} do not provide the required ordinary Chow correspondence. The distinction between these two cycle groups is explicit in that source, including Question 1.11. We have not replaced the ordinary Chow group in condition (2) by its \'etale version.

exact_canonical_statement_tex:
SA06:C.5a: C.5a (Proved: products over $\overline{\mathbb F}_p$ vanish integrally).. Let $k=\overline{\mathbb F}_p$. For every smooth projective $X/k$, the group $\mathrm{CH}^r(X)_{\mathrm{alg}}$ is both torsion and divisible. Algebraic equivalence is generated by pushforwards of degree-zero divisor classes on smooth projective curves under correspondences. Each such Jacobian point is defined over a finite field and is therefore torsion. Multiplication by any positive integer, including $p$, is surjective on the $k$-points of a Jacobian: the corresponding isogeny is surjective as a morphism of varieties over an algebraically closed field. Its images, and sums of these images, are divisible. This proves both assertions. If $\alpha,\beta$ are algebraically trivial cycle classes, choose $m>0$ with $m\alpha=0$, and choose $\gamma$ with $\beta=m\gamma$. Bilinearity gives \[ \alpha\cdot\beta=\alpha\cdot(m\gamma)=(m\alpha)\cdot\gamma=0. \] The identical argument applies to external products on two varieties. There are no inverted primes in this proof. In particular the assertions $1^\circ$ and $1^\circ\mathrm{bis}$ of 14:126 hold integrally modulo rational equivalence over $\overline{\mathbb F}_p$.

SA06:C.5b: C.5b (Known theorem and proved deductions: the Albanese kernel over $\overline{\mathbb F}_p$).. For a smooth projective connected $X/k$ as above, \[ \operatorname{alb}_X:\mathrm{CH}_0(X)^0\xrightarrow{\sim}A_X(k) \] is an integral isomorphism. The precise opened input is \citet[Theorem 1.2]{cySpiessSzamuely2003}: it applies to a smooth variety admitting a smooth compactification over an algebraic closure of a finite field, and gives the full Albanese isomorphism on degree-zero Suslin homology. For proper $X$ that homology is $\mathrm{CH}_0(X)^0$, and $X$ is its own compactification. This includes the $p$-primary part. The prime-to-$p$ assertion of their Theorem 1.1, or prime-to-$p$ Rojtman alone, would not suffice. For an abelian variety the inverse is $x\mapsto[x]-[0]$, so this map is additive and the assertions $4^\circ$, $4^\circ\mathrm{bis}$ hold. Assertion $5^\circ$ is precisely the displayed theorem. The canonical identity $\operatorname{Alb}(X\times Y)=A_X\times A_Y$ gives $6^\circ$. The kernel generators in $2^\circ$ and the rectangle relations in $3^\circ$, $3^\circ\mathrm{bis}$ vanish by C.5a. Thus all members of the chain hold over $\overline{\mathbb F}_p$, integrally. We make no assertion that $\mathrm{CH}_0(X/\mathbb F_q)^0=A_X(\mathbb F_q)$ for an arbitrary finite-field model: the theorem just used is over its algebraic closure.

SA06:C.5c: C.5c (Proved explicit complex rectangle of infinite order).. Let $E/\overline{\mathbb Q}$ be the elliptic curve $y^2=x^3-x$ with origin $O$. Choose $t,s\in\mathbb C$ algebraically independent over $\overline{\mathbb Q}$ and square roots in $\mathbb C$, and put \[ P=(t,\sqrt{t^3-t}),\quad Q=(s,\sqrt{s^3-s}),\quad S=E\times E. \] Then \begin{equation} z=[P,Q]-[P,O]-[O,Q]+[O,O]\in\mathrm{CH}_0(S) \end{equation} has infinite order and Albanese class zero.

SA06:C.5d: C.5d (Refuted over $\mathbb C$: every universal member of the chain).. The two divisor classes $\mathrm{pr}_1^*([P]-[O])$ and $\mathrm{pr}_2^*([Q]-[O])$ on $S$ are algebraically trivial and their product is $z$. This refutes $1^\circ$. Their external product refutes $1^\circ\mathrm{bis}$; the same $z$ lies in the kernel of both projections, refuting the rectangle and product assertions $2^\circ,3^\circ,3^\circ\mathrm{bis}$ and $6^\circ$. For $A=S$, put $x=(P,O)$ and $y=(O,Q)$. Then \[ [x+y]-[x]-[y]+[0]=z\ne0, \] so $x\mapsto[x]-[0]$ is not a group homomorphism, refuting $4^\circ$. The Albanese kernel contains $z$, refuting $4^\circ\mathrm{bis}$ and $5^\circ$. All these are failures with integral coefficients and survive tensoring with $\mathbb Q$. The superscript $a$ on $A_0$ in 14:126 means the algebraically trivial \emph{subgroup} of the rational Chow group. Reading it as the quotient modulo algebraic equivalence would erase the problem.

SA06:C.5e: C.5e (Proved universal implication $4^\circ\Rightarrow3^\circ\mathrm{bis}$).. We retain the universal quantifier over abelian varieties in $4^\circ$. For smooth projective curves $C,D$, apply it to $J(C)\times J(D)$. Additivity of the point-to-cycle map kills every rectangle made from points of its two factors. The normalized Poincar\'e divisor on $J(C)\times C$ induces $\mathrm{CH}_0(J(C))^0\to\mathrm{CH}_0(C)^0$ carrying $[a]-[0]$ to the divisor class $a$; the analogous correspondence exists for $D$. Applying their external product sends the killed rectangle to any prescribed product of two degree-zero divisor classes on $C,D$. Such products therefore vanish. Any two points on a smooth projective connected variety over an algebraically closed field can be joined by a connected chain of curves; after normalizing the components, their difference is a sum of pushforwards of differences on smooth projective curves. Apply the curve result to each pair and push to $X\times Y$. Every rectangle on $X\times Y$ vanishes, proving the implication. Using $4^\circ$ only for one fixed abelian variety would not suffice.

exact_canonical_statement_tex:
SA06:D.1a: D.1a (Proved): exact criterion for a rational slope to restrict to $\mu _2$.. Let $M$ be any subgroup of the group of Weil $q$-numbers, or any subgroup of its quotient by roots of unity, containing $e=q$. A prime $\mathfrak p$ over $p$ gives the additive map \[ s_{\mathfrak p}:M\longrightarrow\mathbb Q, \qquad s_{\mathfrak p}(\lambda)= \frac{v_{\mathfrak p}(\lambda)}{v_{\mathfrak p}(q)}. \] It satisfies $s_{\mathfrak p}(e)=1$ and $s_{\mathfrak p}(m)+s_{\mathfrak p}(cm)=w(m)$. A restriction of this rational cocharacter to $\mu _2$, compatible with the usual restriction of every integral cocharacter and with clearing odd denominators, exists exactly when \[ s_{\mathfrak p}(M)\subset\mathbb Z_{(2)} =\{a/b\in\mathbb Q:b\text{ odd}\}. \tag{D.1} \] In that case it is unique and its dual is the homomorphism $a_{\mathfrak p}:M\to\mathbb F _2$ given by reduction of $s_{\mathfrak p}$ modulo $2$.

SA06:D.1b: D.1b (Proved): the largest simultaneous domain.. For a Galois-stable group $M$, put \[ M^{(2)}=\{m\in M:s_{\sigma\mathfrak p}(m)\in\mathbb Z_{(2)} \text{ for every }\sigma\in\operatorname{Gal}(\overline{\mathbb Q}/\mathbb Q)\}. \tag{D.2} \] This is the largest Galois-stable subgroup on which all the slope restrictions exist. The set $\{a_{\sigma\mathfrak p}\}$ is a canonical Galois-equivariant packet on $D(M^{(2)})$. It is independent of the prime initially chosen, since changing the prime permutes the orbit. This assertion concerns the quotient group $D(M)\to D(M^{(2)})$, or equivalently the subcategory with that character group, and does not assert that its fibre functors extend to the original category.

SA06:D.1c: D.1c (Refuted, with exact repair): the proposed $D(\mathbb Q)$ remedy.. Passing to the rational-slope protorus does not manufacture the missing restriction. Indeed \[ \operatorname{Hom}(\mu _2,D(\mathbb Q)) =\operatorname{Hom}(\mathbb Q,\mathbb Z/2)=0. \tag{D.3} \] Every homomorphism on the right vanishes because $x=2(x/2)$. Thus the canonical map $D(\mathbb Q)\to\mathbb G_m$ has no lift of the nontrivial element of $\mathbb G_m[2]$. Rational slopes do define $D(\mathbb Q)\to T$, as in the Newton homomorphism of \citet[Introduction and \S4]{D_Kottwitz1985}; they do not define a polarizing $\mu _2$-homomorphism through this source. Lead D1 is false if it claims that this cover solves the parity problem or that even slope denominators preclude real fibre functors. The correct restriction source is $D(\mathbb Z_{(2)})$, on exactly the subcategory (D.2).

SA06:D.1d: D.1d (Proved, computed): the requested $q=25$ example.. Let $\varpi=2+i$, $q=25$ and $\lambda=5\varpi^2=15+20i$. In $\mathbb Z[i]$ we have \[ (5)=(\varpi)(\overline\varpi),\quad v_{\varpi}(\lambda)=3,\quad v_{\overline\varpi}(\lambda)=1, \quad\lambda\overline\lambda=625=q^2. \] Set $u=\lambda/q=\varpi/\overline\varpi$. The torsion-free group generated by $q$ and $\lambda$ is $M=\mathbb Ze\oplus\mathbb Zf$, with $e=q$, $f=u$; its weight map is $(2,0)$ and conjugation is $(e,f)\mapsto(e,-f)$. The associated $\mathbb Q$-torus is $\mathbb G_m\times R^1_{\mathbb Q(i)/\mathbb Q}\mathbb G_m$. The two slope maps are $(1,1/2)$ and $(1,-1/2)$. Therefore \[ M^{(2)}=\mathbb Ze\oplus2\mathbb Zf, \qquad a_{\mathfrak p}(e)=a_{\mathfrak p}(2f)=1. \] The two polarizations of the original real torus are $(a(e),a(f))=(1,0)$ and $(1,1)$; neither restricts to the displayed slope parity on $M^{(2)}$. Its real fibre gerbe nevertheless has two isomorphism classes: the kernel of $\varepsilon$ is the compact one-dimensional torus and $H^1(\mathbb R,R^1_{\mathbb C/\mathbb R}\mathbb G_m)=\mathbb Z/2$. All these arithmetic and parity statements are verified by \texttt{code/verify\_examples.py}, whose output is included. This example also shows why saying merely that the rational slope is ``not integral'' is too weak: odd denominators are harmless, whereas this denominator is $2$.

SA06:D.1e: D.1e (Proved): the full category versus a finite subcategory.. In the full Weil-number group, $e=q$ is twice $\sqrt q$; its class modulo roots of unity is still twice that class. Hence $a(e)=1$ is impossible on the full connected group. In the conditional motivic setting of R3 there is no unmodified real fibre functor on the full category, for any $q$. On the full even-weight subgroup modulo roots of unity there is, in contrast, a canonical parity $a=w/2\bmod2$. It is the only parity with $a(e)=1$: its weight-zero subgroup is divisible, since all roots of a weight-zero Weil number are again weight-zero Weil numbers, and every homomorphism from a divisible group to $\mathbb F _2$ vanishes. These statements do not depend on a choice of slope. They are consistent with the uniqueness statement for parity-one polarizations on weight-zero motives in \citet[Lemma 2.46]{Milne1994}. Thus a request for a ``privileged packet'' without specifying slope compatibility has no unique mathematical meaning; with the compatibility of 15:123 it has the exact obstruction D.1a. There is nevertheless a useful alternative that works for every $q$ on every finite-type even-weight subcategory. Namely $a_0=w/2\bmod2$ is defined there, is Galois invariant, and is preserved by every automorphism respecting $w$ and $e$. The splitting $M=\mathbb Ze\oplus\ker(w/2)$ makes the kernel of $\varepsilon$ a compact real torus. By D.0b the real gerbe is neutral, and the R8 correspondence selects the fibre-functor class belonging to $a_0$. This gives a canonical singleton packet from the even grading alone. In D.1d it is $(a(e),a(f))=(1,0)$. It is not slope-compatible: it takes $2f$ to zero, whereas the admissible slope packet takes $2f$ to one. Thus the existence of an alternative Galois-invariant selection does not repair the undefined restriction of the original slope.

Its rational orbits are precisely the orbits on (D.4) of the finite group \[ \overline{\mathcal A}_{\mathbb Q} =\operatorname{im}\bigl(\{A\in\operatorname{GL}(M):Ae=e,\ wA=w, \ A\delta=\delta A\ (\delta\in\Delta)\} \longrightarrow\operatorname{GL}(M/2M)\bigr). \tag{D.5} \] For a possibly disconnected group of multiplicative type with character module $N$, the corresponding answer uses the image in $\operatorname{GL}(M/2M)$ of Galois-equivariant automorphisms of $N$ preserving $e,w$, where $M=N/N_{\mathrm{tors}}$. A rational automorphism must preserve the three distinct rational Galois eigenspaces. Preservation of $e$ forces the invariant eigenline to be fixed, and integral invertibility forces multiplication by $\pm1$ on the other two lines. Thus the only changes on polarizations are the exchange of $a(x)$ and $a(y)$; $a(t)$ is fixed. The four polarizations form exactly two rational orbits, \[ \{(0,1,0),(1,0,0)\},\qquad \{(0,1,1),(1,0,1)\}. \] The torus is connected, so this also refutes transitivity for $\operatorname{Aut}(G,\varepsilon,j)$. For a general infinite-rank character module the same automorphism action on $\operatorname{Hom}(M,\mathbb F_2)$ gives the exact orbit relation, but we do not assert the finite-rank transitivity theorem without that hypothesis.

SA06:D.4b: D.4b (Proved as an equivalence; finite-field conclusion conditional): the effectivity claim.. An algebraic number which is a unit away from its residue characteristic is integral exactly when these valuations are nonnegative. exact_canonical_statement_tex:
SA06:E.1a: E.1a (Proved: saturation as a precise polarity).. Let $G/\mathbb Q$ be a reductive algebraic group, with its category of finite-dimensional rational representations. Let $\mathcal I$ be the set of complex cocharacters, modulo conjugation if desired. For $C\subset\mathcal I$ and a class $\mathcal E$ of representations, define \[ \begin{split} E(C)&=\{V:\text{every weight of every }\nu\in C \text{ on }V_{\mathbb C}\text{ is nonnegative}\},\\ I(\mathcal E)&=\{\nu:\text{every weight of }\nu \text{ on every }V\in\mathcal E \text{ is nonnegative}\},\\ \operatorname{Sat}(C)&=I(E(C)). \end{split} \] Then $\operatorname{Sat}$ is extensive, monotone, and idempotent, and $E(\operatorname{Sat}(C))=E(C)$. The exact missing condition is \begin{equation} C=I(E(C)). \end{equation} The saturated cocharacter sets are in inclusion-reversing bijection with the full representation subcategories that are intersections of the $P(\nu)$. Additional positivity, Tate-twist, weight-zero, and Galois-invariance axioms are imposed on the objects on both sides; they do not replace \eqref{eq:effective-saturation}.

SA06:E.1b: E.1b (Proved lattice form).. For a torus with character lattice $M$ and cocharacter lattice $N=\operatorname{Hom}(M,\mathbb Z)$, assume $C\subset N$ is Galois stable. Then \[ C^\vee=\{m\in M:\langle m,c\rangle\ge0\quad\forall c\in C\}, \qquad \operatorname{Sat}(C)= \{v\in N:\langle m,v\rangle\ge0\quad\forall m\in C^\vee\}. \] To check that rational representations detect every listed character, we take the representation whose weights are the finite Galois orbit of $m$. Galois stability of $C$ makes the whole orbit effective exactly when $m$ is in $C^\vee$. For a split connected reductive group, the same formula works on a maximal torus for a Weyl-stable cone: move $m$ into a dominant chamber; the irreducible representation of highest weight $m$ has all its weights in the convex hull of its Weyl orbit. The Weyl-stable polar therefore makes that whole representation effective. Over $\mathbb Q$ we use a rational representation containing the finite Galois orbit, with multiplicity if descent requires it; multiplicities do not change inequalities.

SA06:E.1c: E.1c (Refuted automaticity for additive cones).. We give complete data compatible with the normalization $\langle\varepsilon,j\rangle=2$. Let \[ T=\mathbb G_m\times R^1_{\mathbb Q(i)/\mathbb Q}\mathbb G_m, \qquad N=\mathbb Z^2, \qquad \overline{(a,b)}=(a,-b), \quad \varepsilon=(1,0)\in M, \quad j=(2,0)\in N. \] Set \[ C=\mathbb N(1,1)+\mathbb N(1,-1) =\{(a,b)\in\mathbb Z^2:a\ge |b|, a\equiv b\pmod2\}. \] It is an additive Galois-stable cone, contains $j$, and has $\varepsilon$ strictly positive away from the origin. The character $\varepsilon$ is in the interior of its real polar. Its integral polar is $C^\vee=\{(u,v):u\ge|v|\}$, because the two generator inequalities are $u+v\ge0$ and $u-v\ge0$. Therefore \[ \operatorname{Sat}(C)=\{(a,b):a\ge|b|\}\supsetneqq C; \qquad (1,0)\in\operatorname{Sat}(C)\setminus C. \] The two cones define exactly the same effectivity structure. This is a counterexample to automatic saturation under the additive-cone requirements alone. Even imposing root saturation is not enough. The monoid \[ C_{\mathrm{open}}=\{0\}\cup \{(a,b)\in\mathbb Z^2:a>|b|\} \] is root saturated: $nv\in C_{\mathrm{open}}$ for an integer $n>0$ implies $v\in C_{\mathrm{open}}$. It has the same integral polar and the same bipolar as $C$, but omits $(1,1)$ and $(1,-1)$. Thus the required saturation includes closure as detected by integral half-spaces, not merely divisibility in the cocharacter lattice.

SA06:E.1d: E.1d (Proved automaticity under a stronger meaning of ``cone'').. There is an important qualification to the preceding answer. Suppose ``cone'' is defined in advance to mean $C=K\cap N$, where $K\subset N_{\mathbb R}$ is a closed convex cone and $\varepsilon$ lies in the interior of $K^\vee$. Then $C$ is saturated as above, in particular when $K$ is rational polyhedral. The conclusion holds without rational polyhedrality: a separating normal for a lattice point outside $K$ can be perturbed into the interior of $K^\vee$ while keeping its value negative at that point, then approximated by a rational normal and scaled to an integral character. This character is nonnegative on $K\cap N$ and excludes the point from the integral bipolar. For completeness, the perturbation uses $m_t=m+t\varepsilon$ for sufficiently small $t>0$, where $m\in K^\vee$ satisfies $\langle m,v\rangle<0$. Since $\varepsilon$ is interior, $m_t$ is interior; a sufficiently close rational point remains there and remains negative on $v$. The separating-hyperplane theorem supplies $m$ because $K$ is closed and convex. This proves both inclusions of the integral bipolar. Thus the manuscript's unspecified quotation-marked ``c\^one'' matters. Saturation is not a consequence of the stated additive requirements; it is automatic if the stronger closed-convex-lattice definition is already part of those requirements. Formula \eqref{eq:effective-saturation} removes that ambiguity entirely. It also gives the strongest exact classification requested in E.1.

SA06:E.3h: E.3h (Refuted: integral equality with ordinary Abel--Jacobi equivalence).. There exists a smooth projective complex fourfold $X$ and an algebraically trivial codimension-three cycle $z$ such that \[ \operatorname{AJ}(z)=0, \qquad z\notin N^3(X). \] By E.3g this $z$ comes from an abelian family integrally. Hence the integral equality of equivalence relations asserted on the right side of Lead E4 is false. The same failure occurs for some $d$-fold in every codimension $3\le i\le d-1$, $d\ge4$. We use the exact opened input of \citet[Corollary 4.2 and Remark 4.3, author p.~10]{cyOttemSuzuki2020}. They construct a smooth threefold $W$, a rank-one degeneracy locus of a map \[ \mathcal O^{\oplus3}\longrightarrow \mathcal O(1,2,0)\oplus\mathcal O(1,0,2) \quad\hbox{on }\mathbb P^1\times\mathbb P^2\times\mathbb P^2, \] and an elliptic curve $E$, for which $X=W\times E$ has a surjective regular Walker map and the isogeny $\alpha:J_W^3(X)\to J_a^3(X)$ has nonzero finite kernel. More precisely, their construction takes coordinates $[S:T]$ on the first factor and the rank-one locus of the matrix \[ \begin{pmatrix} P_1&Q_1&R_1\\ SP_2+qP_3&SQ_2+qQ_3&SR_2+qR_3 \end{pmatrix}. \] Here $q$ is a sufficiently large auxiliary prime, and the three triples of rational-coefficient polynomials have tridegrees $(1,2,0)$, $(0,0,2)$ and $(1,0,2)$, respectively, with the generality and specialization conditions imposed in their Theorem 3.1. These are the exact construction data in that theorem, not a selected numerical example. Their Theorem 3.1 supplies $W$ over $\mathbb Q$ with torsion-free integral cohomology and a nonalgebraic integral Hodge class; their Theorem 4.1 supplies $E$. We use this as a proved primary theorem, not as a claim that we have independently verified their full degeneration argument or selected numerical coefficients for $W,E$. E.3r below gives a fully displayed geometric generic matrix and Legendre elliptic curve to which this obstruction transfers integrally, and supplies a nonzero cycle of order two. Choose $0\ne b\in\ker\alpha$ and use surjectivity to choose $z$ with $\psi_W(z)=b$. Then $\operatorname{AJ}(z)=0$, while E.3g gives $N^3(X)\subset\ker\psi_W$, so $z\notin N^3(X)$. This is the complete deduction from the stated primary input. For $d\ge4$ and $3\le i\le d-1$, put $s=d-4$, $j=i-3$ and take $z'=z\times t^j$ on $X\times\mathbb P^s$. Its Abel--Jacobi image is zero by functoriality. If $z'$ belonged to $N^i$, then multiplication by $t^{s-j}$ followed by projection would put $z$ in $N^3(X)$, by functoriality of Albanese equivalence. Since $0\le j\le s$, the projection is exactly $z$, a contradiction.

SA06:E.3k: E.3k (Refuted: the unqualified integral biconditional in Lead E4; proved corrected fixed-target criterion).. For the fourfold $X=W\times E$ of E.3h, the map $\mathrm{CH}_0(W)\to\mathbb Z$ is an isomorphism by \citet[Lemma 2.4, author p.~4]{cyOttemSuzuki2020}. Fix $w_0\in W(\mathbb C)$. For every point $(w,e)$, the equality $[w]=[w_0]$ on $W$, pushed into $W\times\{e\}$, shows that its zero-cycle class is represented on $\{w_0\}\times E$. Thus this curve supports $\mathrm{CH}_0(X)$, and E.3j proves the family-map converse for every codimension-three abelian family on this $X$. E.3h simultaneously gives an algebraically trivial cycle from an abelian family that is Abel--Jacobi trivial but is not Albanese trivial. The two assertions declared equivalent in the literal integral Lead E4 therefore have different truth values on the same smooth projective fourfold. This refutes that biconditional, while leaving E.3c's rational formulation intact. For an arbitrary smooth projective complex $X$, a precise fixed-target criterion uses \[ K_W^i(X)=\ker\bigl(P^i(X)\longrightarrow J_W^i(X)(\mathbb C)\bigr). \] The integral family-map converse is exactly the assertion that no nonzero image $u_Z(A(\mathbb C))$ of an abelian family is contained in $K_W^i(X)$. Indeed such containment is equivalent to $\phi_{W,Z}=0$, which is equivalent to $a({}^tZ)=0$: one direction uses the finite-kernel argument in E.3i, and the other the cylinder map in E.3b. The rational criterion in E.3c is equivalently $K_W^i(X)\otimes\mathbb Q=0$, because \[ 0\longrightarrow K_W^i(X)\longrightarrow \ker\overline{\operatorname{AJ}} \longrightarrow\ker\alpha\longrightarrow0 \] is exact and $\ker\alpha$ is finite; surjectivity on the right follows from surjectivity of $\psi_W$. Neither condition follows merely from regularity or from the existence of a universal regular homomorphism. We do not identify $P^i(X)$ with the Walker Jacobian in general.

SA06:E.3m: E.3m (Proved: the exact integral Walker reformulation of the general family converse).. Fix a smooth projective complex variety $X$ and a codimension $i$. The following assertions are equivalent: \begin{enumerate} \item For every abelian variety $A$ and every normalized $Z\in\mathrm{CH}^i(A\times X)$, the vanishing $a({}^tZ)=0$ implies $u_Z=0$ integrally. \item The natural surjection $P^i(X)\to J_W^i(X)(\mathbb C)$ is an isomorphism. \item $N^i(X)=\ker\psi_W$ in $\mathrm{CH}^i(X)_{\mathrm{alg}}$. \end{enumerate} These equivalent fixed-target conditions are refuted universally by E.3u below. Their exact common condition is the Walker-kernel equality, which differs from the false integral ordinary Abel--Jacobi equality in Lead E4. We write $J=J_W^i(X)$, $P=P^i(X)$, and $\overline\psi:P\twoheadrightarrow J(\mathbb C)$. The equivalence of (2) and (3) follows from surjectivity of $\psi_W$ and E.3g's inclusion $N^i\subset\ker\psi_W$. Condition (2) implies (1) by E.3i. We prove the other direction. \emph{Choose one family covering the Walker Jacobian.} Assume (1). Every algebraically trivial cycle is an integral point of an abelian family by E.3g. The corresponding regular Walker maps have abelian-subvariety images which generate $J$. A finite sum of these images is all of $J$: otherwise one can successively enlarge their dimensions, which is impossible after $\dim J$ strict enlargements. Thus a product of finitely many such parameter varieties gives an abelian family \[ u_B:B(\mathbb C)\longrightarrow P,\qquad \phi_B=\overline\psi\,u_B:B\twoheadrightarrow J. \] If $J=0$, (1) immediately kills every family and hence $P$; we may therefore assume $\dim J>0$. Let $B_0=(\ker\phi_B)^0$. The restricted family on $B_0$ has zero Walker map and therefore zero cohomological action by E.3b--i. Condition (1) gives $u_B(B_0(\mathbb C))=0$. Consequently $u_B$ factors through $D=B/B_0$, and $D\to J$ is an isogeny. Its abstract kernel on $P$ is a subgroup of the finite group $\ker(D\to J)(\mathbb C)$. Over $\mathbb C$ this subgroup is the point group of a finite subgroup scheme $H\subset D$. Put $E=D/H$. We obtain \[ u_E:E(\mathbb C)\hookrightarrow P, \qquad \lambda:E\twoheadrightarrow J, \qquad \overline\psi\,u_E=\lambda, \] where $\lambda$ is an isogeny and $u_E$ is injective. At this point $u_E$ is a homomorphism of groups; we have not assumed that a universal integral cycle exists on $E\times X$. \emph{Every abelian-family image is already this one.} For any other abelian family $u_A:A(\mathbb C)\to P$, take the sum family on $B\times A$ and repeat the preceding construction. Its Walker map is still surjective. We get an abelian variety $E'$ isogenous to $J$ and an injection $u_{E'}:E'(\mathbb C)\hookrightarrow P$ whose image is $u_B(B(\mathbb C))+u_A(A(\mathbb C))$. The inclusion $B\to B\times A$ induces an algebraic homomorphism $B\to E'$. It kills the kernel of $B\to E$, because its composition with the injective map $u_{E'}$ is $u_B$. Quotient descent therefore gives an algebraic homomorphism $E\to E'$. It is injective on complex points, again by the injections into $P$. Both abelian varieties have dimension $\dim J$, so this homomorphism is an isomorphism. It follows that $u_A(A(\mathbb C))\subset u_E(E(\mathbb C))$. Using E.3g once more gives \[ P=u_E(E(\mathbb C)). \] Moreover, the preceding quotient construction shows that every composite $u_E^{-1}u_A:A\to E$ is an algebraic homomorphism, not merely an abstract homomorphism on points. The kernel of $\overline\psi$ is now the finite group $\ker\lambda(\mathbb C)$. But it is also $\ker\psi_W/N^i(X)$, a divisible group by \citet[Theorem 2.3, author p.~12]{cyACMVWalker2022}. A finite divisible group is zero. Hence $\lambda$ is an isomorphism and (2) follows. This already completes the equivalence; no universality assumption on the Walker map has entered the argument. \emph{Regularity of the resulting quotient, also checked directly.} Let \[ q:\mathrm{CH}^i(X)_{\mathrm{alg}}\longrightarrow P \xrightarrow{u_E^{-1}}E(\mathbb C). \] For a pointed smooth projective parameter variety $(T,t_0)$ and a correspondence $W$, its point-to-cycle map modulo $N$ factors integrally through $\operatorname{Alb}(T)(\mathbb C)$, because $W_*$ kills the Albanese kernel by the definition of $N$. Denote the resulting homomorphism to $E(\mathbb C)$ by $v$. E.3a constructs an integer $m>0$ and an abelian family on $\operatorname{Alb}(T)$ whose map to $P$ is $m$ times the original one. Thus $mv$ is an algebraic homomorphism $f:\operatorname{Alb}(T)\to E$. We check that $v$ itself is algebraic. For every $a\in\operatorname{Alb}(T)[m](\mathbb C)$, $f(a)=mv(a)=v(ma)=0$. In characteristic zero this means that $f$ kills the whole finite group scheme $\operatorname{Alb}(T)[m]$. Hence $f$ factors algebraically through $[m]$ as $f=g\circ[m]$ for a homomorphism $g:\operatorname{Alb}(T)\to E$. The difference $v-g$ takes values in $E[m](\mathbb C)$; its source is divisible, so this finite-valued homomorphism is zero. Therefore $v=g$. Composing with the pointed Albanese map proves regularity for projective parameter varieties. For a smooth quasi-projective parameter variety, choose a smooth projective compactification and close the correspondence; the refined fibres on the original open are unchanged. This reduces regularity to the preceding case. General smooth finite-type parameter schemes can be covered by such opens, and the resulting morphisms agree because their complex-point maps agree and the target is separated. Thus $q$ is a regular homomorphism in the usual sense. We have, in particular, \[ \psi_W=\lambda\circ q. \] The direct regularity check is consistent with the alternative isogeny-initiality proof from the same Theorem 2.3, but that alternative is unnecessary after the finite-divisible-kernel argument. The assertion that the original family converse holds for every $X,i$ remains unproved here.

Its fibres at $a=0,1$ are smooth. Direct enumeration in the supplied program gives respectively $6$ and $9$ rational points. Their Frobenius polynomials on $H^1$ are \[ T^2+5,\qquad T^2+3T+5. \tag{E.5} \] The first Newton polygon has slopes $1/2,1/2$; the second has slopes $0,1$. Thus their rational contravariant crystalline realizations over $\overline{\mathbb F}_5$ are nonisomorphic, and a fortiori their integral $F$-crystals are nonisomorphic. After forgetting Frobenius, both underlying $W(\overline{\mathbb F}_5)$-modules are free of rank two and are isomorphic. The point counts, nonsingularity discriminants, and polygons give every hypothesis of this example.

SA06:E.5d: E.5d (Proved as a classification of the indicated structures): what the crystalline moduli mean.. Let $k=\overline{\mathbb F}_p$, $W=W(k)$, $K_0=\operatorname{Frac}W$, and let $\sigma$ be Witt Frobenius. For an unramified reductive group with fixed smooth model $\mathcal G/\mathbb Z_p$, an isocrystal with a chosen trivial underlying $G$-torsor is represented by $b\in G(K_0)$; $F=b\sigma$. A change of trivialization $g$ changes $b$ to $g^{-1}b\sigma(g)$. Isomorphism classes are therefore the corresponding $\sigma$-conjugacy classes $B(G)$. This is the convention underlying \citet[Introduction and \S\S3--4]{D_Kottwitz1985}. If a dominant Hodge type $\mu$ is fixed, lattices in this fixed isocrystal are the points \[ X_\mu(b)=\{g\mathcal G(W): g^{-1}b\sigma(g)\in\mathcal G(W)\mu(p)\mathcal G(W)\}. \tag{E.6} \] Here a coset represents the lattice $gW^d$ in a faithful representation with its tensors. Applying $F$ to the lattice gives exactly the double-coset condition displayed, so (E.6) follows directly by changing a basis. This is the set defined in \citet[\S1.2.9, author-PDF p.~14]{Kisin2017}. Isomorphism classes after forgetting the embedding in the fixed isocrystal require also quotienting on the left by \[ J_b(\mathbb Q_p)=\{h\in G(K_0):h^{-1}b\sigma(h)=b\}; \] compare \citet[\S1.2.12, author-PDF p.~14]{Kisin2017}. Thus a moduli problem with Frobenius and integral lattices is distinct from $H^1$ of the ordinary group of an unstructured fibre functor. Lead E3 captures one possible source of variation inside a Newton stratum, but cannot explain all variation on 15:193: (E.5) varies the Newton stratum itself. We have not identified the phrase ``la partie continue du $H^1$'' with a defined cohomology object in the manuscript.

SA06:E.5e: E.5e (Proved): unstructured integral fibre functors under a smooth model.. Let $k$ be algebraically closed of characteristic $p$, let $W=W(k)$, and let $\mathcal G/W$ be a smooth affine group scheme of finite presentation. Then $H^1_{\rm fpqc}(W,\mathcal G)=1$. Indeed a $\mathcal G$-torsor $P$ is affine, smooth and of finite presentation over $W$. Its special fibre is nonempty, because the torsor map is faithfully flat, and has a $k$-point because $k$ is algebraically closed. Smoothness lifts that point successively to compatible points over $W/p^m$; the completeness of $W$ and finite presentation of the affine scheme $P$ identify their inverse limit with a $W$-point. A torsor with a point is trivial. Consequently two existing $W$-valued fibre functors whose isomorphism torsor has this group are isomorphic after forgetting $F,V$ and any additional filtration. This proves precisely why ordinary smooth torsor cohomology cannot explain nonisomorphism in that case. The crystalline nonisomorphism in E.5c is a statement about $F$-crystals, not a statement about those unstructured torsors. If the proposed integral motivic group has no such smooth model, or if the isomorphisms are required to commute with Frobenius, this vanishing argument has different hypotheses and does not apply. More generally, let $k$ be perfect of cohomological dimension at most one, and assume in addition that the special fibre $\mathcal G_k$ is connected. Then \citet[Theorem 1.9, p.~51]{D_Steinberg1965} gives $H^1(k,\mathcal G_k)=1$. The same lifting argument proves $H^1(W(k),\mathcal G)=1$. This applies in particular when $k$ is finite, and also to a smooth affine group over $\mathbb Z_\ell$ with connected special fibre. It verifies the finite-stage uniqueness assertion of R16 with its actual hypotheses. It gives no such conclusion from perfection alone, as E.5b shows. Even these finite-stage hypotheses do not alone justify a passage to a pro-group, as the following example shows.

SA06:E.5a: E.5a (Known, with the required derivation): uniqueness over an algebraically closed field.. Let $k$ be algebraically closed, and let $\mathcal C$ be a neutral Tannakian category over $k$, without a tensor-generation or cardinality restriction. Then any two $k$-valued fibre functors are isomorphic. Consequently, whenever the pro-gerbe $T_\infty$ of 15:191 is an affine Tannakian fibre gerbe and one such point is supplied by the indicated realization, it has exactly one isomorphism class of $k$-points.

SA06:E.5b: E.5b (Refuted, with a perfect-field counterexample): passing to the limit does not remove $H^1$.. Let \[ k=\bigcup_{m\geq0}\mathbb F_3(t^{1/3^m}),\qquad L=\bigcup_{m\geq0}\mathbb F_9(t^{1/3^m}),\qquad T=R^1_{L/k}\mathbb G_m. \] The fields are perfect and $L/k$ is a separable quadratic extension. The right $T$-torsor $P$ defined by $N_{L/k}(z)=t$, with action by multiplication, is nontrivial. The neutral category $\operatorname{Rep}_k(T)$ therefore has at least two nonisomorphic fibre functors, even for the constant inverse system.

SA06:E.5f: E.5f (Refuted, including the $\operatorname{cd}(k)\leq1$ refinement): individually trivial finite restrictions need not admit compatible trivializations.. Indeed $\overline{\mathbb F}_3$ is algebraically closed and $\operatorname{trdeg}_{\overline{\mathbb F}_3}k=1$, so the assertion follows from \citet[Lemma 59.95.4, Tag 0F0T]{D_Stacks0F0T}. Every finite stage $G_n=\mathbb G_m$ is smooth and connected and has trivial $H^1(k,G_n)$. For $n\geq0$ put $b_n=1$ if $3\mid n$ and $b_n=0$ otherwise. Take the trivial right $G_n$-torsor $P_n=\mathbb G_{m,k}$, but give these torsors the equivariant transition maps \[ P_{n+1}\longrightarrow P_n,\qquad x_{n+1}\longmapsto t^{b_n}x_{n+1}^2. \tag{E.5.2} \] Then $P=\varprojlim P_n$ is an actual affine fpqc $G$-torsor, and $P(k)=\varnothing$. In particular the forgetful fibre functor on $\operatorname{Rep}_k(G)$ and its twist by $P$ are isomorphic on every finitely generated tensor subcategory but are not isomorphic on the whole category.

SA06:E.5g: E.5g (Proved): conditions that do permit the passage to the limit.. Let $(G_n,P_n)$ be a countable inverse system of affine groups and equivariant torsors of finite type over a perfect field $k$ with $\operatorname{cd}(k)\leq1$. Suppose each $G_n$ and every kernel of $G_{n+1}\to G_n$ are smooth and connected, and the group transitions are faithfully flat. Then each $P_n(k)$ is nonempty by \citet[Theorem 1.9]{D_Steinberg1965}; the fibre over any point of $P_n(k)$ is a torsor under the indicated kernel and so has a $k$-point by the same theorem. Thus $P_{n+1}(k)\to P_n(k)$ is surjective. Inductively choosing compatible points proves $(\varprojlim P_n)(k)\ne\varnothing$. The counterexample (E.5.1) has disconnected transition kernels $\mu_2$, so it does not satisfy this sufficient condition. There is also a compactness criterion, requiring no connectedness condition on the transition kernels. For any directed inverse system, if each $P_i(k)$ is a nonempty compact Hausdorff space and the transition maps are continuous, the product of these spaces is compact. The equations defining compatible points are closed and have the finite intersection property: for finitely many equations choose a common upper index and any point there. exact_canonical_statement_tex: [Proved under stated hypotheses: fixed-boundary finite generation] Let $X$ be normal, proper and connected over an algebraically closed field $k$, let $Y\subsetneq X$ be closed, and let $Q(X,Y)$ be $\pi_1(X\setminus Y)$ modulo the closed normal subgroup generated by wild inertia at the codimension-one components of $Y$. The group $Q(X,Y)$ is topologically finitely generated in each of the following cases: $X$ is projective; $\operatorname{char}k=0$; or $X$ is regular and $Y$ is a normal-crossings divisor. Consequently D.2(ii) holds when the proper compactification is projective, and it holds for every regular proper compactification. || [Known: all surfaces over the algebraic closure of a finite field] D.1 holds in dimension at most two over $\overline{\mathbb F}_p$. So does D.2(ii), including possibly nonnormal proper schemes. || [Proved: a quasi-projective neighborhood of the entire boundary] Let $X$ be normal, connected and proper over an algebraically closed field. If the closed subset $Y\subsetneq X$ is contained in one quasi-projective open subscheme $N\subset X$, then $Q(X,Y)$ is topologically finitely generated. In particular, D.2(ii) holds when the omitted set consists of a single closed point, even on a nonprojective singular proper scheme. More generally, D.2(ii) holds for a possibly nonnormal proper scheme $Z$ whenever its entire codimension-two omitted subset has a quasi-projective open neighborhood in $Z$.

All $R^q h_*G$ for $q>0$ are zero. || [Known sufficient condition; proved numerical equivalence on a smooth base] Assume $f$ has relative dimension one, $S$ is noetherian and excellent, and $G$ is a locally constant constructible sheaf of vector spaces over a finite field $\Lambda$ of characteristic $\ell$, invertible on $S$. Set \[ w_G(s)=\sum_{y\in Y_{\bar s}}\operatorname{Sw}_y(G|_{V_{\bar s}}). \] If $w_G$ is locally constant, every $R^i h_*G$ is locally constant and its formation commutes with arbitrary base change. exact_canonical_statement_tex: [Known: the invertible-prime arithmetic $K(\pi,1)$ theorem] Let $K$ be a number field, let $S$ be a finite set of finite places, and let $X=\operatorname{Spec}\mathcal O_K\setminus S$. For every prime $\ell$ invertible on $X$, the pro-$\ell$ completion of the \'etale homotopy type of $X$ is a $K(\pi,1)$. In particular, all of its higher homotopy pro-groups, including its second one, vanish. This includes $\ell=2$ when $K$ has real places, on the ordinary \'etale site. || [Proved: arithmetic tame $K(\pi,1)$ for all permitted coefficients] Let $X_0=\operatorname{Spec}\mathcal O_K\setminus S$, let $D$ be any finite reduced divisor on $X_0$, and put $U=X_0\setminus D$. Let $\mathcal L$ be the set of rational primes invertible on $X_0$; equivalently, $\ell\in\mathcal L$ if and only if every place of $K$ above $\ell$ lies in $S$. Let $\pi=\pi_1^t(U/X_0)$ classify finite \'etale covers of $U$ tamely ramified along $D$. For every finite discrete $\pi$-module $M$ whose order has prime divisors in $\mathcal L$, and every $q\geq0$, the comparison is an isomorphism \[ H^q(\pi,M)\xrightarrow{\ \sim\ }H^q_{\mathrm{et}}(U,M). \] The permitted-prime second tame homotopy pro-group is zero: $\Pi_2^{t,\mathcal L}(U/X_0)=0$. Thus every pair $(K,S)$ has the $K(\pi,1)$ property asked for with tame coefficients prime to all residue characteristics of $X_0$. For $K=\mathbb Q$ and $D$ empty, this gives $\Pi_2^t(\operatorname{Spec}\mathbb Z-S)=0$ in that coefficient convention, with allowed primes exactly $S$.

exact_canonical_statement_tex: \label{a:finite} Suppose $\dim X=n\geq4$. Choose $N\geq0$ such that \[ H^i(Y,L^{-m}|_Y)=0\qquad(i=1,2;\ m>N). \] Such an $N$ exists. Restriction gives a canonical identification $\Pic(X)\simeq\Pic(Y_N)$ and an exact sequence \begin{equation}\label{a:exact} 0\longrightarrow H^1(Y,U_N)\longrightarrow\Pic(X) \longrightarrow\Pic(Y)\xrightarrow{\delta_N}H^2(Y,U_N). \end{equation} Consequently the complete answers for this particular pair are \[ \ker(\Pic(X)\to\Pic(Y))=H^1(Y,U_N),\qquad \operatorname{coker}(\Pic(X)\to\Pic(Y))=\operatorname{im}(\delta_N). \] The sheaf $U_N$, with its actual multiplication, has the filtration \[ U_N^{(m)}=1+I^m/I^{N+1},\qquad U_N^{(m)}/U_N^{(m+1)}\simeq L^{-m}|_Y\quad(1\leq m\leq N). \] Thus a finite tower with the additive layers of R4 determines both groups and all obstruction maps. Replacing this tower by the direct sum of the cohomology of its layers is not justified.

exact_canonical_statement_tex: For arbitrary elliptic schemes $E/S$ in characteristic $2$ and ordinary $Q/S$ with a chosen nonzero étale $2$-torsion section, the usual Igusa quotient $X=(E\times Q)/\langle(-1,+P)\rangle$ satisfies \[ \operatorname{Pic}^{\tau}_{X/S}=Y^\vee\times E^\vee[2]. \] It is flat, and the fibrewise Picard variety is $Y^\vee$, compatibly with base change. Both first Hodge numbers are $2$. The torsion Néron--Severi group is $\mathbb Z/2$ on an ordinary fibre of $E$ and zero on a supersingular fibre, since it is the component group of $E[2]$. In the family \eqref{dgj:elliptic-family}, torsion therefore disappears under specialization. This product family is not the full deformation family of the surface. A first-order nonflatness assertion is stated in accessible published literature, but the proof audit below identifies a gap, and D4o subsequently refutes the assertion by computing the full ordinary deformation. For the ordinary Igusa surface $X_0$ put $I=H^1(X_0,T_{X_0})^\vee$ and $R_1=k\oplus I$ with $I^2=0$, and take the first-order deformation whose Kodaira--Spencer class is the identity of $H^1(X_0,T_{X_0})$. Here $T_{X_0}=\mathcal O_{X_0}^{\oplus2}$ and $h^1(\mathcal O_{X_0})=2$, so $\dim_k I=4$. Chai--Oort, \S3.9(iv), printed p.~35 \cite{DGJ_ChaiOort2017}, states that $\operatorname{Pic}^{\tau}_{X_1/R_1}$ is not flat. The source identifies this assertion with Mumford's example. The surface deformation can be taken projective: the obstruction to lifting the square of an ample line bundle is twice its square-zero obstruction, hence zero in characteristic two, and ampleness over an Artinian base is detected on the special fibre.

exact_canonical_statement_tex: The proof argues that the off-neutral component cannot be a flat torsor under the neutral component because their absolute tangent dimensions are five and six, respectively, and their tangent maps to the base have different ranks. That inference is false for torsors under a nonsmooth group. Here is a complete example with exactly those dimensions. Over an algebraically closed field $k$ of characteristic two put \[ R=k[e_1,e_2,e_3,e_4]/(e_i e_j:1\leq i,j\leq4), \qquad P=\operatorname{Spec}R[z]/(z^2-e_1). \] It is finite free of rank two over $R$, with basis $1,z$. The unit $1+z$ satisfies $(1+z)^2=1+e_1$; multiplication on this unit makes $P$ a $\mu_2$-torsor. Explicitly, with $y^2=0$ the coordinate of $\mu_2$, the torsor map is $z_1\mapsto z$, $z_2\mapsto z+y+zy$. On the two free rank-four coordinate modules over $R$ its determinant is $1+e_1$, a unit. This proves the torsor condition, including faithful flatness.

If $P$ were a scheme, an affine neighborhood of their common descended point would pull back to just such an affine neighborhood.

For a relatively ample line bundle $L$ of class $\delta$, write \[ \Phi(L)=R\operatorname{pr}_{B*} (\mathcal P\otimes\operatorname{pr}_A^*L),\qquad F_\delta(L)=\det\Phi(L)^{-1},\qquad \chi=\chi(L). \] These are relative constructions. The complex is perfect; in the ample case it is a vector bundle of rank $\chi$. Tensoring $L$ by a bundle from $S$ changes its determinant by a bundle from $S$ only, so $F_\delta$ defines a morphism of relative Picard sheaves. The theorem of the square gives, up to bundles from the base, \[ (1,\lambda_L)^*\mathcal P =m^*L\otimes\operatorname{pr}_1^*L^{-1} \otimes\operatorname{pr}_2^*L^{-1}. \] Changing variables $(x,a)\mapsto(x+a,a)$ therefore gives $\lambda_L^*\Phi(L)=\pi_*L\otimes L^{-1}$ up to the same harmless base factors. Taking determinants shows $\lambda_L^*F_\delta(L)=L^\chi$ in the relative Picard sheaf. Consequently, if $\delta'$ is the class of $F_\delta(L)$, then \[ \lambda_\delta\lambda_{\delta'}=[\chi]_B, \qquad \lambda_{\delta'}\lambda_\delta=[\chi]_A. \] Indeed the formula for a pulled-back line bundle first gives $\lambda_\delta\lambda_{\delta'}\lambda_\delta =\chi\lambda_\delta$; the isogeny $\lambda_\delta$ is faithfully flat and can be cancelled on the right. Duality gives the other equality. Thus $\delta'$ is positive, whereas the determinant itself has class $\varphi(\delta)=-\delta'$. This proves precisely the negative sign in the box of 59:10.

exact_canonical_statement_tex: Let $k$ be algebraically closed, of any characteristic. Let $j:Y\hookrightarrow X$ be a smooth hyperplane section of a smooth projective $n$-fold, and use the incidence abelian varieties of J1i. Fix $\ell\ne\operatorname{char}k$ and put $r=2i-1$. For a smooth projective $d$-fold $W$, write $L_W$ for cup product by the chosen hyperplane class. The convention for the Lefschetz lowering operator is \[ \Lambda_W(L_W^a v)= \begin{cases}L_W^{a-1}v,&a>0,\\0,&a=0,\end{cases} \qquad v\in H^b_{\rm prim}(W,\mathbb Q_\ell). \] Thus $\Lambda_W$ lowers degree by two and Tate twist by one; it has no extra $\mathfrak{sl}_2$ coefficient. Let $B(W)$ mean that this operator is induced by a rational algebraic correspondence in $\operatorname{CH}^{d-1}(W\times W)_{\mathbb Q}$. With this explicit convention the following implications hold: \begin{enumerate} \item If $2i\leq n-1$ and $B(X)$ holds, then $j^*:P^i_{\rm inc}(X)\to P^i_{\rm inc}(Y)$ is an isogeny. \item If $2i\geq n+1$ and $B(Y)$ holds, then the same homomorphism is surjective. \end{enumerate} Only the relevant degree of $\Lambda_X$, respectively $\Lambda_Y$, is needed. The cohomological inputs are Deligne's hard Lefschetz theorem \cite[Theorem 4.1.1, p.~217]{DGJ_Deligne1980} and weak Lefschetz \cite[(4.1.6), pp.~218--219]{DGJ_Deligne1980}. The coefficient-free lowering convention is also spelled out in \cite[Section 4.1, pp.~6--7]{DGJ_Peters2026}. No integral inverse, equality of incidence and universal regular equivalence, or middle-degree fixed-part assertion is part of this conclusion.

Proposition~\ref{C:noncoherent-positive-boundary} gives a normal local, noncoherent, nonvaluation positive example. Theorem~\ref{C:shallow-full-support-three-torsion} bounds the remaining mixed shallow classes by three, but does not prove their vanishing or the existence of a nonzero class. Proposition~\ref{C:ramified-A2-MF-cancellation} proves cancellation of the specified standard matrix-factorization lattice on every ramified exponent-three dyadic node. Proposition~\ref{C:odd-node-MCM-comparison-boundary} shows that the whole generic Swan kernel is invisible to the ordinary MCM Grothendieck group on odd-exponent dyadic nodes. This resolves this family completely in degree two but does not supply the missing criterion for arbitrary singular bases. Proposition~\ref{C:divisible_nil_invariance} removes nil ideals that are uniquely divisible by all integers, without any noetherian hypothesis, and gives nonreduced mixed-characteristic positive examples. Proposition~\ref{C:reduced_regular_fibres} also excludes a criterion using regularity of the arithmetic fibres alone: the reduced local ring $\mathbb Z_{(2)}[x]_{(2,x)}/(2x)$ has regular generic and special fibres but an infinite degree-two comparison kernel. Regularity of the total ring along the positive-characteristic locus in Theorem~\ref{C:regular_modular_locus} must not be confused with this weaker fibrewise condition. This covers arbitrary modules $J$ and every square-zero thickening of $\mathbb Z_{(2)}$. It removes that whole class from the open gate; higher nilpotent thickenings and general reduced singular mixed-characteristic rings are not classified by it. Proposition~\ref{C:derived_fibre_twins} further shows that the complete family of derived prime fibres, the rational fibre, and all integer-localized $K_0$ groups together are insufficient: the two local orders displayed there have identical such data and opposite answers. A general criterion must retain additional information about the total ring or its arithmetic thickenings. Theorem~\ref{C:allprime_squarezero_criterion} removes the whole square-zero class over every unramified mixed-characteristic DVR: for every prime $p$ and every module $J$, the condition is that $p:J\to J$ be bijective, and every failure is detected in degree $p$. Proposition~\ref{C:odd_torsion_allheights} includes torsion of every finite height and $p$-divisible torsion; its proof detects the same fixed class at every finite stage by a primary curvature-length invariant over $A/p^m$. Theorem~\ref{C:ramified_torsion_infinite} further excludes every ramified square-zero module containing torsion of the full ramification height, at every prime, and proves that its explicit induced class has infinite order even modulo the polynomial image. This strengthens every unramified torsion witness to infinite order. In contrast, Proposition~\ref{C:cyclotomic_torsion_cancellation} proves that the rank-one witness cancels after induction when the base contains a primitive odd-prime root of unity and the ideal is killed by that root minus one. Proposition~\ref{C:cyclotomic_matrix_cancellation} extends this cancellation to every infinitesimal deformation of a direct sum of constant cyclotomic characters. It does not prove polynomiality in that remaining case. Theorem~\ref{C:cyclotomic_flat_criterion} uses a nonsplit integral lattice to settle every flat module over a DVR with $\zeta_p-1$ a uniformizer: again $pJ=J$ is necessary and sufficient. Thus the square-zero DVR gate is now the ramified odd-prime directions not excluded by the stated tests, including this cyclotomic residue-torsion case. Higher nilpotent thickenings and arbitrary reduced singular bases remain outside these classification theorems.

SA23-A-04: Let $k\subset K$ be fields of characteristic zero, let $n\geq1$, and put $A=K[[t_1,\ldots,t_n]]$. The ordinary $A$-module $\Omega_{A/k}$ is not projective, and therefore is not free. Consequently $A$ is not formally smooth over $k$ for the discrete topology. In particular this holds for $\mathbf Q[[t]]/\mathbf Q$ and for every case of A.1 with finite-dimensional $\Omega_{K/k}$.

SA23-A-05: This proves the positive-dimensional presumption of cote 22/023 without assuming finite transcendence degree of $K/k$. The two supplied witnesses give either $\dim A>0$ or a doubtful $\dim A\geq0$. If the latter includes $n=0$, that reading is false: every characteristic-zero field extension is formally smooth and its differentials form a free vector space \cite[Tag 031U, Proposition 10.158.9]{rootStacksFields}. The same-field non-smoothness assertion is located by secondary literature at Matsumura, \emph{Commutative Ring Theory}, p.~215; that page has not yet been opened, so we rely on the complete proof above and make no novelty claim.

SA23-A-08: Let $k\subset K$ be fields of characteristic $p>0$ and let $n\geq1$. The following conditions are equivalent: \begin{enumerate} \item $K[[t_1,\ldots,t_n]]$ is formally smooth over $k$ for the discrete topology. \item $K/k$ is separable and $[K:K^p]<\infty$. \end{enumerate} If (2) holds and a $p$-basis $c_1,\ldots,c_r$ of $k$ extends to a $p$-basis $c_1,\ldots,c_r,b_1,\ldots,b_s$ of $K$, then $\Omega_{K[[t_1,\ldots,t_n]]/k}$ is free on $db_1,\ldots,db_s,dt_1,\ldots,dt_n$.

Take $k=K=\mathbf F_p(s_1,s_2,\ldots)$, where the $s_i$ are algebraically independent. The relative $p$-basis is empty, but for $n\geq1$ the power series ring is not formally smooth over $k$. If $k$ is perfect and $K/k$ is separable, the manuscript's finite-relative-$p$-basis criterion is correct, and the infinite case has a negative answer.

If its transcription ``nul en degr\'es $0$'' means vanishing of $H_0$, it says instead $(f)=R$. For a proper ideal it is never satisfied. If it means the degree-zero term of the complex is zero, it forces $R=0$. The original typescript has the same visible gap before the digit $0$; a positive-degree sign cannot be recovered from the visible ink. The positive-homology interpretation is independently fixed by the proposed final EGA remark and by the SGA definition. \cite[physical PDF pp.~53--54, archive footer pp.~52--53]{algManuscript23} \cite[IV 19.1.8, p.~189]{algEGAIV4} \cite[VII 1.1, p.~416]{algSGA6}

SA23-C-2: Put $I=(f_1,\ldots,f_r)$. If $f$ is $M$-Koszul-regular, the natural map of graded modules \[ (M/IM)[T_1,\ldots,T_r]\longrightarrow \bigoplus_{n\ge0}I^nM/I^{n+1}M,\qquad T_i\longmapsto f_i, \] is an isomorphism. In particular, if $M=R$, $I/I^2$ is free of rank $r$ over $R/I$, with the displayed generators as basis, and $\operatorname{Sym}_{R/I}(I/I^2)\to\operatorname{gr}_I R$ is an isomorphism. Ordinary regular sequences are Koszul-regular. The ring case is also \cite[VII, Proposition 1.3, p.~418]{algSGA6}; the proof below gives the arbitrary-module form.

SA23-C-6: For finite modules over Noetherian local rings and sequences in the maximal ideal, ordinary, Koszul, and quasi-regularity are equivalent (Stacks Project, Lemma 15.31.7, tag \texttt{062D}; opened). \cite[Lemma 15.31.7]{algStacksKoszul} The word ``local'' cannot be dropped for sequences: in the Noetherian ring $k[x,y]\times k[x,y]$ the sequence $((x,1),(y,0))$ is regular, whereas the reversed sequence begins with a zerodivisor. Its final quotient is $k$. The failure in Example~\ref{SA23-C-5} is the failure of Nakayama for an infinitely generated homology module: $xM=M\ne0$. For a sequence in the maximal ideal of a local ring $R$, if the positive Koszul homology modules of every prefix are finite, acyclicity of the full sequence does imply ordinary $R$-regularity. Indeed, the cone long exact sequence shows that multiplication by the last element is surjective on the positive homology of the preceding complex; Nakayama kills it. Repeating this argument reduces to a one-element complex. This gives a valid finiteness replacement for the false unrestricted converse. The Noetherian case satisfies that replacement. SGA 6 VII, Proposition 1.7(iii), explicitly retains a Noetherian hypothesis for precisely this converse; Proposition 1.7(i)--(ii) records the two unrestricted transitivities proved above. \cite[Expos\'e VII, Proposition 1.7, p.~422]{algSGA6} For comparison, a different local nonpermutation example is \cite[Example 10.68.3]{algStacksNonpermutation}; the scheme-theoretic transitivities are also stated in \cite{algStacksImmersions}.

SA23-C-8: Let $R$ be any ring, let $I=(f_1,\ldots,f_r)$, and let $M$ be any $R$-module. If $\operatorname{Ext}^j_R(R/I,M)=0$ for $j<r$, then $f$ is $M$-Koszul-regular. If in addition $R$ is Noetherian local, $I$ is proper, and $M$ is finite and nonzero, $f$ is an ordinary $M$-regular sequence. This proves the auxiliary lemma on cote 23, scans 063--064, in its inherited Noetherian setting, and gives a valid Koszul version without that setting.

Thus its associated object for either of the displayed actions is the same natural bundle, obtained from their common restricted $G$-action. The construction consequently cannot be an equivalence: it sends two nonisomorphic $H$-actions to isomorphic natural bundles. This explains exactly why pointed jets use augmented automorphisms. The whole solution groupoid, including the possibility that it is empty, is the groupoid of functions $c:\Gamma\to H$ satisfying \[ c|_\pi=1,\qquad c(\gamma)\theta_\gamma(c(\delta))t(\gamma,\delta) =c(\gamma\delta), \] modulo the action $c(\gamma)\mapsto h c(\gamma)\theta_\gamma(h^{-1})$ of $H^\pi=Z_H(\alpha_0(\pi))$. In the topological case require that $\gamma\mapsto c(\gamma)s(\gamma)$ be continuous; if $s$ is continuous this is equivalent to continuity of $c$. Thus existence itself is expressed by explicit equations from the given extension, without choosing a solution in advance. If an extending section $\alpha:\Gamma\to E$ exists, let $\gamma\cdot h=\alpha(\gamma)h\alpha(\gamma)^{-1}$ be the resulting action on $H$. Then the groupoid of extending sections, with conjugations that preserve $\alpha_0$, is \[ \bigl[Z^1(\Gamma,H;\pi)/H^\pi\bigr], \quad Z^1(\Gamma,H;\pi)= \{c:\Gamma\to H:\ c(\gamma\delta)=c(\gamma) (\gamma\cdot c(\delta)),\ c|_\pi=1\}. \] Here $h\in H^\pi$ acts by $c(\gamma)\mapsto h c(\gamma)(\gamma\cdot h^{-1})$. If $\pi$ is normal, this groupoid is canonically $[Z^1(\Gamma/\pi,H^\pi)/H^\pi]$; its set of isomorphism classes is $H^1(\Gamma/\pi,H^\pi)$. The identifications depend on the reference section $\alpha$; changing it twists the coefficient action.

cat:J2: Suppose $\pi\triangleleft\Gamma$, $\Gamma/\pi=\mathbf Z$, and $H^\pi=G'_L(L)$. Write $\sigma$ for the action of $1\in\mathbf Z$ on $G'_L(L)$ induced by a fixed extending section. The extensions are classified by the $\sigma$-conjugacy classes \[ G'_L(L)/\bigl(b\sim h b\sigma(h)^{-1}\bigr). \] The automorphism group of the class represented by $b$ is $\{h\in G'_L(L):h b=b\sigma(h)\}$.

cat:J4: Let $k$ be any perfect field of characteristic $p$, $L=W(k)[1/p]$, and $\sigma$ Witt Frobenius. Rank-one isocrystals over $L$ are classified by \[ L^\times/\{\sigma(c)/c:c\in L^\times\}. \] There is a split exact sequence of abelian groups \[ 1\longrightarrow W(k)^\times/\{\sigma(u)/u:u\in W(k)^\times\} \longrightarrow H^1(\mathbf Z,L^\times) \xrightarrow{v_p}\mathbf Z\longrightarrow0, \] whose splitting sends $n$ to $[p^n]$. If $k$ is algebraically closed, the left term is trivial, so slopes classify rank-one isocrystals.

Over an arbitrary affine base $Y=\operatorname{Spec}R$, the complete classification is instead the groupoid of triples \[ (P_0,P_\infty,\phi),\qquad \phi:P_0\otimes_{R[t]}R[t,t^{-1}] \xrightarrow{\sim}P_\infty\otimes_{R[t^{-1}]}R[t,t^{-1}], \] where the two modules are finitely generated projective of rank $n$; morphisms are pairs of module isomorphisms intertwining $\phi$. Equivalently, all objects can be specified explicitly by idempotent matrices $e_0\in M_r(R[t])$ and $e_\infty\in M_s(R[t^{-1}])$ of constant rank $n$, and rectangular Laurent matrices $U\in M_{s\times r}(R[t,t^{-1}])$, $V\in M_{r\times s}(R[t,t^{-1}])$ satisfying \[ U=e_\infty Ue_0,\quad V=e_0Ve_\infty,\quad VU=e_0,\quad UV=e_\infty. \] Here $r,s$ range over all finite integers; they are not extra invariants of the bundle. Morphisms are invertible maps between the images of the two pairs of idempotents which commute with $U$ on the overlap. Thus the classification does not presuppose that projective modules over $R[t]$ or $R[t^{-1}]$ have already been classified or are free. For general $Y$, these data are descended along an affine open covering. Principal $\mathrm{GL}_n$-bundles have exactly this classification.

geo-Kh-jump: On $\mathbf P^1_k\times\mathbf A^1_k$ take the extension $0\to\mathcal O(-1)\to E\to\mathcal O(1)\to0$ whose class is the coordinate $s$ in $H^1(\mathbf P^1,\mathcal O(-2))\otimes_k k[s]\simeq k[s]$. At $s=0$ it is $\mathcal O(-1)\oplus\mathcal O(1)$. At a nonzero field-valued point the boundary map after twisting by $-1$ is multiplication by $s$ from $H^0(\mathcal O)$ to $H^1(\mathcal O(-2))$. Consequently $H^0(E(-1))=0$, and the field classification with degree zero forces $E\simeq\mathcal O^2$. This is the precise obstruction behind treating (h) as just a list of integers independent of the base. The extension is locally free because it is an extension of locally free sheaves.

cat:L6: For the corresponding flat formal groupoid and Lie coalgebroid of Theorem~\ref{cat:L5}, differentiation gives an equivalence between stratifications on arbitrary $A$-modules and integrable $P$-connections. It preserves tensor products and its underlying functor on $A$-modules is the identity.

cat:L7: Filter the relative de Rham complex of the source map by total order, where an augmentation-ideal factor and a one-form both have order one. Let $K_n$ be its quotient by total order greater than $n$. The augmentation $K_n\to A$ is a quasi-isomorphism for every $n$. The same statement holds for the linearized complex of any stratified coefficient module, with augmentation to that module. Consequently \[ R\!\varprojlim_n K_n\simeq A \] in the derived category of sheaves, and likewise with coefficients. For modules over a ring the ordinary inverse-limit complex also computes this derived limit. For arbitrary sheaves that last assertion requires a derived-limit-acyclicity hypothesis on the degreewise towers and is not asserted without it.

cat:L8: For a flat formal groupoid, let its formal descent site mean the site of the nilpotent jets of its simplicial nerve, with all simplicial and jet-transition maps as morphisms, and coverings induced by the chosen topology on the base. A crystal on this site means a module cartesian for these transition maps. Such crystals are exactly stratified modules and hence, by Theorem~\ref{cat:L6}, modules with integrable coalgebroid connection. The finite-order resolution and its derived completion are those of Proposition~\ref{cat:L7}. More concretely, if $X\to S$ is a smooth morphism of $\mathbf Q$-schemes and the groupoid is the formal completion of $X\times_SX$ along its diagonal, this equivalence is the usual crystalline starting equivalence: crystals of $\mathcal O$-modules on the nilpotent infinitesimal site of $X/S$ are equivalent to $\mathcal O_X$-modules with integrable $S$-connection. In characteristic zero the nilpotent divided-power crystalline site has the same objects, because divided powers are uniquely $x^{[n]}=x^n/n!$.

exact_canonical_statement_tex:
cat:L1: Let $P$ be an $A$-module. The data defining a degree-one graded derivation $d$ of $\Lambda_A^\bullet P$ are an additive derivation $d_0:A\to P$ and an additive map $d_1:P\to\Lambda_A^2P$ satisfying \[ d_1(a\omega)=d_0(a)\wedge\omega+a d_1(\omega). \] There is a unique such extension $d$. It is a differential if and only if \[ d_1d_0=0\quad\hbox{and}\quad d_2d_1=0, \qquad d_2=d|_{\Lambda_A^2P}. \] The first equation alone is insufficient, even for a free module of rank three over $\mathbf Q$.

cat:L2: If $P$ is finite projective and $T=P^\vee$, the differentials of Proposition~\ref{cat:L1} correspond bijectively to $A$-Lie algebroid structures on $T$. Explicitly the anchor $\theta:T\to\operatorname{Der}_{\mathbf Q}(A,A)$ and bracket are \begin{align*} \theta(X)(a)&=\langle d_0a,X\rangle,\\ \langle\omega,[X,Y]\rangle &=\theta(X)\langle\omega,Y\rangle -\theta(Y)\langle\omega,X\rangle -\langle d_1\omega,X\wedge Y\rangle. \end{align*} Here a Lie algebroid means a $\mathbf Q$-Lie bracket, an $A$-linear Lie-homomorphism anchor, and $[X,aY]=a[X,Y]+\theta(X)(a)Y$.

cat:L3: For an adic formal category over $\mathbf Q$ with $P$ flat over $A$, the canonical surjection \[ \operatorname{Sym}_A^nP\longrightarrow I^n/I^{n+1} \] is an isomorphism for every $n\geq0$. Each $B/I^{n+1}$ is flat over $A$ for both $s$ and $t$.

cat:L4: Every formal category in Lemma~\ref{cat:L3} is a formal groupoid. Its inversion is uniquely determined by composition and identity.

cat:L5: Over a ringed topos of $\mathbf Q$-algebras, the functor taking an adic formal category in the preceding pro-algebra sense, with flat $I/I^2$, to its invariant de Rham complex is an equivalence with the category of pairs \[ (P,d),\qquad P\text{ flat},\quad d:\Lambda_A^qP\longrightarrow\Lambda_A^{q+1}P, \quad d^2=0, \] where $d$ is a degree-one derivation. The arrow convention on the formal side is a continuous coordinate-proalgebra map $B\to B'$ over $A$, respecting source, target, identity and composition. On the differential side it is a map $\Lambda_A^\bullet P\to\Lambda_A^\bullet P'$ over $A$ commuting with the differential. Thus if arrows on the formal side are instead written as geometric maps $G\to H$, the equivalence is contravariant: their pullbacks go from the coordinate algebra and invariant forms of $H$ to those of $G$. The construction is also functorial for compatible changes of $A$. The inverse integrates the Lie coalgebroid. Finite projectivity is unnecessary.
